idiom_name: std::function hook registry with RAII registration token
implementation_notes: POSA2's home language: the abstract Interceptor interface collapses into std::function<Result(Context&)> stored per event name in a std::vector/std::map, the Dispatcher is the class or free function that walks that container and forwards the context, and RAII handles replace manual lifecycle management - registration returns a token whose destructor unregisters, so attachment ends exactly when the owner dies. The classic abstract-class form (virtual event_callback plus a Dispatcher hierarchy) is still justified when the framework is shipped as a binary library with an ABI-stable virtual interface, which is precisely why ACE keeps it.
pitfalls: A hook that registers or removes another hook mutates hooks_ while fire() iterates it: vector reallocation invalidates the iterators and references - queue mutations and apply them after the walk.
Dangling captures: a hook capturing this stays valid as long as it is registered, which is easily outlived by the framework - unregister in the destructor (RAII) or capture a weak_ptr.
std::function erases the type at the cost of an indirect call plus a possible heap allocation for large captures; use a plain function pointer or a resolved handler for hot events.
Iterating a std::map adds pointer chasing per event; keep the per-event list flat when dispatch is hot.

variants.name: ACE service objects over the Service Configurator (classic)
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's original industrial realization: ACE ships the framework roles as reusable classes and lets services be linked into a running process (ACE_Service_Object with init/suspend/resume/fini hooks, configured by ACE_Service_Config from a svc.conf description), so interceptor lifecycles are managed by the framework's configuration rather than by hand. Choose it when ACE's other frameworks are already in the stack; the std::function chain is smaller and type-safe for new code.
pitfalls: The service lifecycle (init/suspend/resume/fini) is driven by the configuration framework: leaking a suspended service keeps it registered and it resumes on the next reload.
ACE couples interceptors to its own Reactor/Service-Configurator machinery, which is a large dependency for what a std::function chain can do in a few lines.
